title: behavioral interviews STAR and authentic experience narratives
concepts: Behavioral interviews ask for specific past examples to understand how a candidate thinks, acts, collaborates, and learns in situations relevant to the role.

Prepare a small story bank drawn from real work, study, or community experience. Each story should be adaptable to several competencies without changing the facts or claiming another person's work as your own.
STAR(R) organizes a concise answer as Situation, Task, Action, Result, and Reflection. Spend most of the time on your own actions and reasoning, then give a specific result and what you learned.
Use concrete evidence when available: scope, users, time, quality, reliability, or a measurable change. If no metric exists, state an observable outcome honestly instead of inventing a number.
Strong answers make ownership clear while recognizing teammates. Explain tradeoffs and uncertainty, respond to follow-up questions directly, and reflect on what you would change.

Some prompts are hypothetical or situational rather than retrospective. Clarify the conditions, state assumptions, explain a practical approach, and identify how you would communicate and evaluate the result.

scopeExclusions: Company-specific hiring rubrics, scoring algorithms, and confidential interview banks are excluded.
Technical coding, DSA, system design, and code-review interview content belongs to other curriculum topics.
Resume writing, compensation negotiation, and recruiter outreach are outside this behavioral-interview topic.
Candidates must use genuine experience; do not invent achievements, metrics, or confidential details.
